title: Multi-Stack Portfolio Architecture Study
description: In 2007 I built my personal portfolio three times using Classic ASP/VBScript, JSP/Java, and PHP so I could directly compare server-side web technologies. All three versions used the same MySQL schema, frontend, content, graphics, CSS, and JavaScript, and switching implementations changed little more than the URL and backend syntax. The exercise helped me determine which server-side stack I wanted to use going forward, and I ultimately standardized more heavily on PHP.

sections.title: One Portfolio, Three Backends
paragraphs: I designed the portfolio once and then implemented the server-side layer independently in three technologies.
The user-facing application remained effectively identical across all three versions.

sections.title: Shared Frontend
paragraphs: All three versions used the same frontend assets and presentation.

sections.title: Shared MySQL Database
paragraphs: Each backend implementation connected to the same MySQL database and schema.
Skills and portfolio categories were read dynamically from MySQL rather than being duplicated separately for each server implementation.

sections.title: No Framework
paragraphs: I did not use a web framework.
I created my own reusable/component-like organization so the presentation and content could remain consistent while the server-side implementation changed underneath it.

sections.title: Direct Technology Comparison
paragraphs: The purpose of the project was to learn the differences between the major server-side technologies I was considering for future work.
Because each version implemented the same application against the same database, I could compare the stacks directly rather than comparing unrelated tutorials or sample projects.

sections.title: Mostly Syntax Differences
paragraphs: The comparison showed me that the three server-side stacks were fundamentally solving many of the same problems.
Moving the application between ASP/VBScript, JSP/Java, and PHP required mostly syntax changes rather than major architectural redesign.

sections.title: Interchangeable Implementations
paragraphs: From the user's perspective, switching between implementations produced almost no visible difference.
The primary external difference was the URL and server technology handling the request.

sections.title: PHP Became My Preferred Stack
paragraphs: After implementing the same application in all three environments, I preferred PHP and increasingly used it for later web development.
The decision came from direct comparative implementation rather than choosing a backend based only on documentation or popularity.

sections.title: Public Portfolio
paragraphs: The portfolio was publicly hosted for several years.
The original hosting location or domain is no longer remembered.

sections.title: Historical Portfolio Role
paragraphs: This is primarily a historical learning and architecture project rather than a flagship modern portfolio item.
It is still useful as evidence of early full-stack development, database-driven web applications, and comparative technology evaluation.
